title: Enabling Preference-driven Unlearning in Few-step Distilled Text-to-Image Diffusion Models

paper.title: Enabling Preference-driven Unlearning in Few-step Distilled Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Text-to-image diffusion models are increasingly distilled into few-step variants and being deployed to enable fast inference. However, their ability to generate harmful or undesired content poses significant safety risks. Data-driven unlearning methods suppress targeted generations by fine-tuning model weights using specialized unlearning objectives. Crucially, these objectives implicitly rely on multi-step denoising dynamics, an assumption that breaks down for few-step distilled (FSD) models, resulting in ineffective forgetting. Furthermore, performing unlearning on the non-distilled base model and subsequently re-distilling it to obtain an unlearned FSD model incurs substantial computational and time overhead, making it impractical in many settings. Hence, we address this limitation with a preference-driven unlearning framework that revisits Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) for diffusion models. We show that standard DPO and its unlearning derivatives, formulated around noise-prediction error, transfer poorly to FSD models due to their altered generation dynamics. To overcome this, we introduce a modified preference optimization formulation explicitly aligned with the few-step generation properties, enabling direct concept removal in FSD models while preserving few-step efficiency and maintaining strong retention of desirable (non-targeted) capabilities. We evaluate our framework primarily on identity and NSFW (nudity) removal tasks and also extend our method to object-level unlearning. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent and effective forgetting, and strong retention performance, establishing our method as a practical and principled solution for unlearning in FSD models.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text-to-image ( T2I ) diffusion models underpin modern generative visual synthesis, enabling high-quality and controllable image generation Zhang et al. (2023) ; Saharia et al. (2022) ; Rombach et al. (2022) ; Pernias et al. (2023) . However, their success has amplified concerns about undesirable generations Park et al. (2024) ; Birhane et al. (2023) ; Rando et al. (2022) ; Schramowski et al. (2023) ; Golatkar et al. (2024) , driven by unsafe or identity-specific content in large-scale training data Schuhmann et al. (2022) . Open-weight Stable Diffusion ( SD ) models Rombach et al. (2022) , widely accessible via HuggingFace [ 42 ] , can generate celebrity identities or not-safe-for-work ( NSFW ) content such as nudity. Safety filters are often bypassable via prompt obfuscation or multilingual cues Yang et al. (2024a) ; Liu et al. (2024) ; Schramowski et al. (2023) ; Tsai et al. (2024) ; Yang et al. (2024b) , motivating targeted unlearning to remove specific concepts while preserving utility Bourtoule et al. (2021) ; Liu et al. (2024) ; Gandikota et al. (2023) ; Gandikota et al. (2024) ; Park et al. (2024) ; Fan et al. (2023) ; Ko et al. (2024) ; Wu and Harandi (2025) ; Patel and Qiu (2025) ; Wu and Harandi (2024) ; Gong et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2024d) . Concurrently, T2I models are distilled into few-step variants Song et al. (2023) ; Luo et al. (2023) ; Sauer et al. (2024b) ; Sauer et al. (2024a) ; Yin et al. (2024b) ; Yin et al. (2024a) ; Chadebec et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2024) ; Zhou et al. (2025) ; Zhou et al. (2024) ; Chen et al. (2025a) for efficient inference. These few-step distilled ( FSD ) models reduce sampling from 50–100 sampling steps Rombach et al. (2022) ; Song et al. (2021) to 2–8 steps, typically via student reparameterization and teacher-guided training Song et al. (2023) ; Luo et al. (2023) . This alters generation dynamics: FSD models commit early with limited intermediate exploration (Figure 1 A ). Also, undesirable concept residues from the base model ( BM ) can transfer to, and even be amplified in, FSD models (Figure 1 B ), making post-distillation safety critical. Figure 1 : A. LPIPS-to-final vs. timesteps for the base model (BM) [ 20 ] and its few-step distilled (FSD) variant [ 19 ] . BM follows long, weakly constrained trajectories, while FSD shows steep LPIPS decay, committing within a few steps, limiting mid-path adaptability. B. Severity of unsafe generations in FSD. FSD model shows elevated detections pre-unlearning compared to its BM, which our method markedly reduces. C. SD-Turbo [ 75 ] unlearning dynamics . Our method (last row) based on consistency error shows stable, gradual and effective unlearning during the course of training. A naïve solution—first unlearning on the BM and then re-distilling—assumes that unlearning effects transfer faithfully through the distillation process Luo et al. (2023) ; Yin et al. (2024a) , an assumption that is not guaranteed in practice Suriyakumar et al. (2025) ; George et al. (2025a) . Moreover, this pipeline incurs substantial computational overhead ( \eg , Luo \etal Luo et al. (2023) report 32 A100 GPU hours, while Yin \etal Yin et al. (2024a) report 36 hours on 72 A100 GPUs). Since the FSD model is ultimately the deployed artifact, it is both necessary and desirable to directly unlearn undesirable properties on the FSD model itself. Preference-based methods such as direct unlearning optimization ( DUO ) Park et al. (2024) and SafetyDPO (AlignGuard) Liu et al. (2025a) that are based on direct-preference optimization ( DPO ) Rafailov et al. (2023) ; Wallace et al. (2024) have shown robust Park et al. (2024) and scalable Liu et al. (2025a) T2I unlearning while enabling fine-grained control Park et al. (2024) ; Helbling et al. (2025) , by contrasting preferred and dispreferred samples using noise-prediction errors along denoising trajectories. However, this formulation assumes full-step diffusion with long trajectories Zhang et al. (2025) and noise-based parameterization Ho et al. (2020) ; Song et al. (2021) ; Rombach et al. (2022) . When applied to FSD models, characterized by few-step generation and different parameterization Luo et al. (2023) ; Karras et al. (2022) , this assumption breaks, yielding ineffective unlearning, see Figure 1 C . We identify this objective dissonance as the key bottleneck. We propose C onsistency- e nforced P reference-driven U nlearning ( CePU ), a framework tailored to FSD models. Instead of noise-prediction error Wallace et al. (2024) , CePU (C-P-U) uses consistency error Song et al. (2023) , \ie , the discrepancy between final timestep predictions from adjacent noisy timesteps, capturing the intrinsic few-step inductive bias Chen et al. (2025b) ; Song et al. (2023) . This consistency error serves as an implicit reward signal, which is minimized for preferred samples and maximized for dispreferred ones, aligning preference learning with FSD dynamics. Notably, directly unlearning on the FSD model achieves performance comparable to unlearning on the BM followed by distillation (Appendix D ), while requiring only ≈ 15 \approx 15 minutes on a single A5000 GPU, highlighting the practicality of post-distillation unlearning. We evaluate CePU on identity removal and nudity suppression, including red-teaming prompts Tsai et al. (2024) ; Yang et al. (2024a) ; Yang et al. (2024b) ; Chin et al. (2024) ; Schramowski et al. (2023) . Since FSD models can generate unsafe content even without explicit prompts (Figure 5 ), this provides a stringent testbed. We further analyze utility–unlearning trade-offs and extend CePU to object-level unlearning. In summary: ❶ We identify a fundamental dissonance between noise-prediction-based preference unlearning objectives and FSD dynamics (Section 2.2 ). ❷ We propose CePU that seeks to alleviate the dissonance with consistency-based rewards aligned with few-step generation (Section 2.4 ). ❸ We demonstrate effective unlearning across identity, nudity, and object-level settings and analyze utility–unlearning trade-off Pareto fronts to understand the trade-offs across various methods and model families (Section 3 ).

However, when applied to FSD models, directly optimizing Diffusion-DPO ( 2 ) (and its unlearning variants Liu et al. (2025a) ; Park et al. (2024) ) yields markedly weaker unlearning, despite identical preference supervision. This discrepancy points to a fundamental objective mismatch. (2020) ; Karras et al. (2022) . sections.heading: 2.3 Rectifying Dissonance via Consistency
sections.text: The preceding analysis reveals a fundamental objective dissonance : ϵ \bm{\epsilon} -error–based rewards do not faithfully reflect the generation dynamics of few-step distilled (FSD) models. Any remedy must therefore (i) respect the output parameterization, \eg , ( 4 ), and (ii) preserve the few-step inductive bias induced by distillation, which the conventional 𝒙 0 {\bm{x}}_{0} -error fails to capture. We address this by operating in the sample space while explicitly encoding few-step structure through consistency . Consistency models Song et al. (2023) enforce a self-consistency mapping 𝒇 ( t ) : 𝒙 t ↦ 𝒙 0 {\bm{f}}^{(t)}:{\bm{x}}_{t}\mapsto{\bm{x}}_{0} along the probability flow ODE Song et al. (2020) ; Song et al. (2023) , such that all points on ODE trajectory map to a common origin: 𝒙 0 = 𝒇 ( t ) ​ ( 𝒙 t ) = 𝒇 ( t ′ ) ​ ( 𝒙 t ′ ) , ∀ t , t ′ ∈ [ 0 , T ] . {\bm{x}}_{0}={\bm{f}}^{(t)}({\bm{x}}_{t})={\bm{f}}^{(t^{\prime})}({\bm{x}}_{t^{\prime}}),\quad\forall t,t^{\prime}\in[0,T]. (5) This property induces few-step generation, as the model is trained to directly predict the 𝐱 0 {\bm{x}}_{0} sample from any noisy timestep Zhang et al. (2024b) ; Chen et al. (2025b) . Then, 𝒇 θ ( t ) ​ ( 𝒙 t ) − 𝒙 0 = ∑ j = 1 m δ θ ​ ( 𝒙 t j ) , ‖ 𝒙 0 − 𝒇 θ ( t ) ​ ( 𝒙 t ) ‖ 2 ≤ m ​ ( ∑ j = 1 m ‖ δ θ ​ ( 𝒙 t j ) ‖ 2 2 ) 1 / 2 . {\bm{f}}_{\theta}^{(t)}({\bm{x}}_{t})-{\bm{x}}_{0}=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\delta_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}),\quad\|{\bm{x}}_{0}-{\bm{f}}_{\theta}^{(t)}({\bm{x}}_{t})\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{m}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{m}\|\delta_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}})\|_{2}^{2}\right)^{1/2}. (6) Proposition 1 (proof in Appendix C.3 ) shows that minimizing stepwise discrepancies ∥ δ θ ( . ) ∥ 2 2 \|\delta_{\theta}(.)\|_{2}^{2} simultaneously reduces 𝒙 0 {\bm{x}}_{0} -error ( ‖ 𝒙 0 − 𝒇 θ ( t ) ​ ( 𝒙 t ) ‖ 2 2 ) \left(\|{\bm{x}}_{0}-{\bm{f}}_{\theta}^{(t)}({\bm{x}}_{t})\|_{2}^{2}\right) while enforcing consistency across timesteps, \ie , 𝒇 θ ( t j ) ​ ( 𝒙 t j ) ≈ 𝒇 θ ( t j − 1 ) ​ ( 𝒙 t j − 1 ) {\bm{f}}_{\theta}^{(t_{j})}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}})\approx{\bm{f}}_{\theta}^{(t_{j-1})}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j-1}}) . sections.heading: 2.4 Consistency-enforced Preference-driven Unlearning ( CePU )
sections.text: Building on the objective dissonance identified above, we seek a preference objective that preserves the likelihood-ratio interpretation of DPO while operating directly on the consistency dynamics that govern few-step generation. The relative likelihood l θ ​ ( 𝒙 0 | 𝒙 t ) l_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{0}|{\bm{x}}_{t}) introduced in Section 2.1 , however, is not directly expressed in terms of the step-to-step behavior optimized by distilled few-step models. We therefore connect the DPO reward to this behavior through the sample-space decomposition in Proposition 1 . Specifically, the proposition below rewrites the relative likelihood exactly as the sum of timestep-local consistency errors and cross-timestep interactions , providing the basis for a tractable consistency-aware preference objective. Proposition 2 . Then the implicit reward l θ ​ ( 𝐱 0 | 𝐱 t ) l_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{0}|{\bm{x}}_{t}) decomposes exactly as: l θ ​ ( 𝒙 0 | 𝒙 t ) = − 1 2 ​ σ t 2 ​ [ ∑ j = 1 m Δ θ C ​ ( 𝒙 t j ) ⏟ timestep-local + 2 ​ ∑ j < k ( ⟨ δ θ ​ ( 𝒙 t j ) , δ θ ​ ( 𝒙 t k ) ⟩ − ⟨ δ ϕ ​ ( 𝒙 t j ) , δ ϕ ​ ( 𝒙 t k ) ⟩ ) ⏟ cross-timestep interactions ] , l_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{0}|{\bm{x}}_{t})=-\tfrac{1}{2\sigma_{t}^{2}}\Big[\underbrace{\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{m}\Delta_{\theta}^{\textup{C}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}})}_{\text{timestep-local}}+\underbrace{2\textstyle\sum_{j<k}\big(\langle\delta_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}),\delta_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{k}})\rangle-\langle\delta_{\phi}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}),\delta_{\phi}({\bm{x}}_{t_{k}})\rangle\big)}_{\text{cross-timestep interactions}}\Big], (7) where Δ θ C ​ ( 𝐱 t j ) = ‖ δ θ ​ ( 𝐱 t j ) ‖ 2 2 − ‖ δ ϕ ​ ( 𝐱 t j ) ‖ 2 2 \Delta_{\theta}^{\textup{C}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}})=\|\delta_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}})\|_{2}^{2}-\|\delta_{\phi}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}})\|_{2}^{2} . Proposition 2 (proof in Appendix C.3 ) is an exact identity and clarifies which components of the likelihood reward can be realized through local consistency training. In particular, the cross-timestep term couples increments from different locations along the trajectory, requires 𝒪 ⁡ ( m 2 ) \mathcal{O}(m^{2}) pairwise interactions, and cannot be estimated from a single sampled adjacent transition. Retaining it would therefore forfeit the simple stochastic training used by DPO. We instead retain the timestep-local component, which is directly estimable from adjacent timesteps, and define the consistency-motivated surrogate reward l ~ θ ​ ( 𝒙 0 | 𝒙 t ) \tilde{l}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{0}|{\bm{x}}_{t}) : l ~ θ ( 𝒙 0 | 𝒙 t ) = − c t ∑ j = 1 m Δ θ C ( 𝒙 t j ) , c t = 1 2 ​ σ t 2 > 0 . \vskip-10.0pt\tilde{l}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{0}|{\bm{x}}_{t})=-c_{t}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\Delta_{\theta}^{\textup{C}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}),\qquad c_{t}=\tfrac{1}{2\sigma_{t}^{2}}>0.\vskip-3.0pt (8) Importantly, l ~ θ \tilde{l}_{\theta} is a heuristic surrogate rather than an approximation with guaranteed sign or ordering relative to l θ l_{\theta} . The two have the same sign whenever the magnitude of the omitted cross-timestep contribution is smaller than that of the timestep-local component (Appendix C.3 ), while the practical validity of this surrogate is evaluated empirically in Section 3 . This choice replaces the conventional noise-prediction reward with Δ θ C ​ ( ⋅ ) \Delta_{\theta}^{\textup{C}}(\cdot) , which directly measures the model’s relative step-to-step consistency against the reference model and therefore aligns preference optimization with few-step generation dynamics . Substituting l ~ θ \tilde{l}_{\theta} for l θ l_{\theta} in the DPO argument in ( 1 ) gives − log ( sig ( β ( l ~ θ ( 𝒙 0 + | 𝒙 t + ) − l ~ θ ( 𝒙 0 − | 𝒙 t − ) ) ) ) = − log ( sig ( − β c t ∑ j = 1 m ( Δ θ C ( 𝒙 t j + ) − Δ θ C ( 𝒙 t j − ) ) ) ) . -\log\left(\text{sig}\left(\beta\left(\tilde{l}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}^{+}_{0}|{\bm{x}}_{t}^{+})-\tilde{l}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}^{-}_{0}|{\bm{x}}_{t}^{-})\right)\right)\right)=-\log\left(\text{sig}\left(-\beta c_{t}\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left(\Delta_{\theta}^{\textup{C}}({\bm{x}}^{+}_{t_{j}})-\Delta_{\theta}^{\textup{C}}({\bm{x}}^{-}_{t_{j}})\right)\right)\right). (9) Furthermore, directly evaluating the complete timestep sum inside sig ​ ( ⋅ ) \text{sig}(\cdot) would still require constructing the full trajectory. To recover stochastic single-step training, we exploit the convexity of − log ⁡ ( sig ​ ( − u ) ) -\log(\text{sig}(-u)) and apply Jensen’s inequality (Appendix, Lemma 2 ), obtaining the per-step upper bound − log ( sig ( − β c t ∑ j = 1 m ( Δ θ C ( 𝒙 t j + ) − Δ θ C ( 𝒙 t j − ) ) ) ≤ − 1 m ∑ j = 1 m log ( sig ( − β m c t ( Δ θ C ( 𝒙 t j + ) − Δ θ C ( 𝒙 t j − ) ) ) ) ) . -\log\left(\text{sig}\left(-\beta c_{t}\sum_{j=1}^{m}(\Delta_{\theta}^{\textup{C}}({\bm{x}}^{+}_{t_{j}})-\Delta_{\theta}^{\textup{C}}({\bm{x}}^{-}_{t_{j}}))\right)\leq-\tfrac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\log\left(\text{sig}\left(-\beta mc_{t}(\Delta_{\theta}^{\textup{C}}({\bm{x}}^{+}_{t_{j}})-\Delta_{\theta}^{\textup{C}}({\bm{x}}^{-}_{t_{j}}))\right)\right)\right). (10) The right-hand side can be optimized by sampling a timestep t j t_{j} rather than evaluating the complete trajectory. Viewing the summation as an expectation over timesteps, absorbing the positive scale m ​ c t mc_{t} into β \beta , and conditioning both preference samples on the undesirable concept prompt 𝒄 − {\bm{c}}^{-} yields our consistency-aware preference objective ℒ C-DPO ​ ( θ ) = − 𝔼 ( 𝒙 t j + , 𝒙 t j − , 𝒄 − , t j ) ​ [ log ⁡ ( sig ​ ( − β ⁡ ( Δ θ C ​ ( 𝒙 t j + , 𝒄 − ) − Δ θ C ​ ( 𝒙 t j − , 𝒄 − ) ) ) ) ] , \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\textbf{{C-DPO}}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}^{+},{\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}^{-},{\bm{c}}^{-},t_{j})}\Big[\log\big(\text{sig}\big(-\beta(\Delta_{\theta}^{\text{C}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}^{+},{\bm{c}}^{-})-\Delta_{\theta}^{\text{C}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}^{-},{\bm{c}}^{-}))\big)\big)\Big], (11) where Δ θ C ​ ( 𝒙 t j , 𝒄 ) = ‖ 𝒇 θ ( t j ) ​ ( 𝒙 t j , 𝒄 ) − 𝒇 θ ( t j − 1 ) ​ ( 𝒙 t j − 1 , 𝒄 ) ‖ 2 2 − ‖ 𝒇 ϕ ( t j ) ​ ( 𝒙 t j , 𝒄 ) − 𝒇 ϕ ( t j − 1 ) ​ ( 𝒙 t j − 1 , 𝒄 ) ‖ 2 2 . \displaystyle\Delta_{\theta}^{\text{C}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}},{\bm{c}})=\|{\bm{f}}_{\theta}^{(t_{j})}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}},{\bm{c}})-{\bm{f}}_{\theta}^{(t_{j-1})}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j-1}},{\bm{c}})\|_{2}^{2}-\|{\bm{f}}_{\phi}^{(t_{j})}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}},{\bm{c}})-{\bm{f}}_{\phi}^{(t_{j-1})}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j-1}},{\bm{c}})\|_{2}^{2}. (12) Thus, ℒ C-DPO \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{C-DPO}} retains the preference-learning structure of ℒ Diff-DPO \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{Diff-DPO}} but replaces its noise-prediction-based likelihood proxy with the consistency-based signal Δ θ C ​ ( ⋅ ) \Delta_{\theta}^{\text{C}}(\cdot) . This resolves the objective dissonance : the preference objective now optimizes the same step-to-step behavior that determines the output of a few-step distilled sampler, as illustrated in Figure 1 C (last row). Preference-based suppression alone, however, does not explicitly constrain the model on non-target concepts and can therefore alter desirable generations. We address this with a complementary consistency-based retention regularizer, ℒ RET ​ ( θ ) = 𝔼 ( 𝒙 t j + , 𝒄 + , t j ) ​ ‖ 𝒇 θ ( t j ) ​ ( 𝒙 t j + , 𝒄 + ) − 𝒇 ϕ ( t j − 1 ) ​ ( 𝒙 t j − 1 + , 𝒄 + ) ‖ 2 2 , \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{RET}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}^{+},{\bm{c}}^{+},t_{j})}\|{\bm{f}}^{(t_{j})}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}^{+}_{t_{j}},{\bm{c}}^{+})-{\bm{f}}^{(t_{j-1})}_{\phi}({\bm{x}}^{+}_{t_{j-1}},{\bm{c}}^{+})\|_{2}^{2}, (13) which anchors the updated model’s few-step prediction on non-target concepts to that of the reference model. Combining targeted preference-driven suppression with this utility-preserving constraint gives the final CePU objective: ℒ CePU ​ ( θ ) = ℒ C-DPO ​ ( θ ) + λ ​ ℒ RET ​ ( θ ) , \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{CePU}}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_{\texttt{C-DPO}}(\theta)+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\texttt{RET}}(\theta), (14) where λ \lambda controls the utility–unlearning Pareto frontier (Section 3.4 ). While ℒ C-DPO \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{C-DPO}} suppresses undesirable generations through consistency-aware preference optimization, ℒ RET \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{RET}} preserves few-step fidelity on non-target concepts, enabling selective unlearning without unnecessarily degrading model utility. Figure 2 B summarizes the overall CePU framework. In practice, the adjacent states 𝒙 t j {\bm{x}}_{t_{j}} and 𝒙 t j − 1 {\bm{x}}_{t_{j-1}} , with t j − 1 = t j − k t_{j-1}=t_{j}-k , are obtained by forward-noising the same clean sample 𝒙 0 {\bm{x}}_{0} using a shared noise realization ϵ \epsilon . This isolates the change across timesteps from variation due to independently sampled noise. The lower-noise prediction 𝒇 θ ( t j − 1 ) ​ ( 𝒙 t j − 1 , 𝒄 ) {\bm{f}}_{\theta}^{(t_{j-1})}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j-1}},{\bm{c}}) is treated as a stop-gradient target, so optimization updates the prediction at t j t_{j} toward a stable adjacent-step target rather than allowing both sides of the consistency relation to move simultaneously. The same construction is used for ℒ RET \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{RET}} ; complete implementation details are provided in Algorithm 1 (Appendix E.2 ).

(2024) ; Park et al. (2024) ; Liu et al. (2025a) ; Miao et al. (2025) , and CePU . We adopt this standard, fully bootstrapped construction following prior work Park et al. (2024) . (2024) ; Wu and Harandi (2025) ; Wu and Harandi (2024) ; Fan et al. (2023) ; Patel and Qiu (2025) ; Gandikota et al. (2024) ; Yoon et al. (2025) ; Huang et al. (2024a) ; Kim et al. sections.heading: 3.3 Object-level Unlearning
sections.text: Beyond identity and nudity removal, we consider object-level unlearning, a standard benchmark in prior works Gandikota et al. (2023) ; Gandikota et al. (2024) ; Thakral et al. (2025b) . In contrast to identity-style settings, preference-based objectives are ill-defined here: there is no canonical preferred counterpart for a target object, leading to ambiguity. As a result, prior preference-based methods, \eg , DUO Park et al. (2024) and SafetyDPO Liu et al. (2025a) , do not evaluate this setting. To resolve this, we adopt a simple strategy inspired by negative preference optimization ( NPO ) Zhang et al. (2024c) , \ie , we omit the positive preference term Δ θ C ​ ( 𝒙 t j + , 𝒄 − ) \Delta_{\theta}^{\text{C}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}^{+},{\bm{c}}^{-}) from ℒ C-DPO \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{C-DPO}} , thereby eliminating the need for a preferred concept example. Hence, the resulting objective ℒ C-DPO object \mathcal{L}^{\text{object}}_{\texttt{C-DPO}} is defined as : ℒ C-DPO object ​ ( θ ) = − 𝔼 ( 𝒙 t j + , 𝒙 t j − , 𝒄 − , t j ) ​ [ log ⁡ σ ⁡ ( − β ⁡ ( Δ θ C ​ ( 𝒙 t j + , 𝒄 − ) − Δ θ C ​ ( 𝒙 t j − , 𝒄 − ) ) ) ] = − 𝔼 ( 𝒙 t j − , 𝒄 − , t j ) ​ [ log ⁡ σ ⁡ ( β ​ Δ θ C ​ ( 𝒙 t j − , 𝒄 − ) ) ] . \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{C-DPO}}^{\text{object}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(\xcancel{{\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}^{+}},{\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}^{-},{\bm{c}}^{-},t_{j})}\Big[\log\sigma\big(-\beta(\xcancel{\Delta_{\theta}^{\text{C}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}^{+},{\bm{c}}^{-})}-\Delta_{\theta}^{\text{C}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}^{-},{\bm{c}}^{-}))\big)\Big]=-\mathbb{E}_{({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}^{-},{\bm{c}}^{-},t_{j})}\Big[\log\sigma\big(\beta\Delta_{\theta}^{\text{C}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}^{-},{\bm{c}}^{-})\big)\Big]. (15) which directly maximizes consistency term Δ θ C ​ ( 𝒙 t j − , 𝒄 − ) \Delta_{\theta}^{\text{C}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}^{-},{\bm{c}}^{-}) , steering the model away from the target concept while remaining bounded via σ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \sigma(\cdot) . We keep the consistency-based regularizer ℒ RET \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{RET}} ( 13 ) as-is to preserve adjacent concepts. Notably, this formulation removes the requirement for coupled preference pairs , allowing 𝒙 + {\bm{x}}^{+} and 𝒙 − {\bm{x}}^{-} to be generated independently based on the decided retain/unlearn object classes. Following prior work Gandikota et al. (2023) ; Gandikota et al. (2024) ; Thakral et al. (2025b) ; Yoon et al. (2025) ; Kumari et al. (2023) , we evaluate on Imagenette [ 43 ] class unlearning. We report target object class accuracy 𝒜 target \mathcal{A}_{\text{target}} , non-target object accuracy 𝒜 other \mathcal{A}_{\text{other}} , LPIPS \mathrm{LPIPS} on non-target generated samples, and the harmonic mean ℋ mean \mathcal{H}_{\text{mean}} between 1 − 𝒜 target 1-\mathcal{A}_{\text{target}} and 𝒜 other \mathcal{A}_{\text{other}} . sections.heading: 3.4 Additional Analysis and Observations
sections.text: Figure 6 : Pareto -plots similar to Figures 3 and 5 with different λ \lambda values on DS-V7-LCM [ 18 ] for for identity unlearning ( Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt ), and nudity unlearning ( I2P prompts). Figure 7 : Pareto -plots showing the unlearning-utility trade-off, similar to Figure 5 of SD-Turbo [ 75 ] on I2P prompts for different sampling steps across β \beta sweeps.

sections.heading: Effect of λ \lambda and β \beta .
sections.text: CePU ( 14 ) includes a utility-preservation regularizer weighted by λ \lambda . We analyze its effects on Pareto curves (Figure 7 ) for identity and nudity (I2P) unlearning. A clear trade-off emerges: increasing λ \lambda improves utility on non-target prompts but weakens unlearning, while smaller λ \lambda strengthens unlearning at the cost of utility. For identity unlearning, λ = 100 \lambda{=}100 achieves a strong balance (near-perfect UA with minimal degradation), while for nudity, λ = 10 \lambda{=}10 yields the best DSR–utility frontier under I2P Schramowski et al. (2023) . Based on this analysis we fixed the λ \lambda value for CePU in all the experiments. The preference temperature β \beta further modulates this trade-off, that allows to operate along the Pareto -curve, with larger β \beta leading to weaker updates and improved utility retention (Figures 3 , 5 , 7 , and 7 ).

sections.heading: Number of sampling steps.
sections.text: To assess robustness to number of generation sampling steps, we perform an ablation over the number of sampling steps while keeping all other training and evaluation settings fixed. Figure 7 compares the resulting Pareto curves for nudity unlearning tasks (I2P prompts). We observe that CePU maintains effective unlearning even in the extreme single-step setting, demonstrating favorable DSR-utility trade-off.

sections.heading: Paired sample generation.
sections.text: We use a fixed SDEdit-generated dataset Meng et al. (2022) ; Park et al. (2024) across all preference-based methods to eliminate sampling variance and ensure fair comparison. Figure 8 : I2P detections vs. LPIPS \mathrm{LPIPS} across edit strengths τ \tau . SDEdit constructs counterfactual pairs by perturbing an image at timestep t = ⌊ τ × T ⌋ t=\lfloor\tau\times T\rfloor and denoising back to t = 0 t=0 , controlled by edit strength τ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \tau\in(0,1) , where T T denotes the pre-set total number of denoising steps which is typically 50 50 when using DDIM Song et al. (2021) sampling. The process is fully self-bootstrapped and yields in-distribution samples, reducing data–model mismatch. We observe that varying τ \tau marginlly affects I2P detections and LPIPS \mathrm{LPIPS} (Figure 8 ), indicating robustness to edit strength. The computational cost is dominated by U-Net evaluations during denoising, with per-pair complexity 𝒪 ⁡ ( ( T + t ) ​ C UNet ) \mathcal{O}((T+t)\,C_{\text{UNet}}) , where C UNet C_{\text{UNet}} denotes a single forward pass. Example pairs are provided in Appendix E.1 .

sections.heading: Generalization across FSD models.
sections.text: While CePU is derived based on the consistency property (Sections 2.3 and 2.4 ), we observe that its applicability is not restricted to the consistency-model family Song et al. (2023) ; Luo et al. (2023) . Empirically, we also observe effective unlearning on SD-Turbo [ 75 ] , which is distilled via score distillation sampling Poole et al. (2023) and adversarial objectives Sauer et al. (2024b) ; Sauer et al. (2024a) ; entirely different from consistency models . This suggests that CePU inherently captures a more general property of FSD models.

sections.heading: Unlearning in T2I diffusion models.
sections.text: Unlearning in diffusion models has emerged as an important direction for the responsible deployment of generative systems Heng and Soh (2023) ; Lyu et al. (2024) ; Lu et al. (2024) ; Lee et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2024a) ; Wu et al. (2025) ; Cai et al. (2025) ; Bui et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2025) ; Han et al. (2025) ; Cywiński and Deja (2025) . Early work such as ESD Gandikota et al. (2023) removes targeted concepts by fine-tuning the U-Net using noise prediction based objectives. CA Kumari et al. (2023) adopts a similar counterfactual fine-tuning strategy, while recently FADE Thakral et al. (2025b) introduces fine-grained unlearning with a prior objective to preserve neighboring concepts. Other directions explore weight-saliency pruning Wu and Harandi (2024) ; Fan et al. (2023) ; Chavhan et al. (2025) , multi-objective optimization for balancing erasure and utility Wu and Harandi (2025) ; Ko et al. (2024) ; Gao et al. (2025a) , meta-learning for faster concept removal Patel and Qiu (2025) ; Patel et al. (2023) ; Gao et al. (2025b) ; Huang et al. (2024b) , and adversarial methods for robust concept erasure Srivatsan et al. (2025) ; Gong et al. (2024) ; Huang et al. (2024a) ; Kim et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2024d) ; Bui et al. (2024) . Complementary works study zero-shot unlearning through closed-form weight updates (UCE) Gandikota et al. (2024) or prompt-embedding manipulation (SAFREE) Yoon et al. (2025) . In our experiments, we evaluate baselines implemented in the HuggingFace’s Diffuser [ 17 ] ecosystem Gandikota et al. (2023) ; Kumari et al. (2023) ; Gandikota et al. (2024) ; Yoon et al. (2025) ; Thakral et al. (2025b) . Methods implemented in the original CompVis framework [ 14 ] such as Wu and Harandi (2024) ; Fan et al. (2023) ; Patel and Qiu (2025) ; Huang et al. (2024a) ; Kim et al. (2024) prevent using HuggingFace checkpoints of FSD models and are therefore not included in this study.

sections.heading: Preference-based unlearning.
sections.text: DPO Rafailov et al. (2023) learns from ranked output pairs via a Bradley–Terry model Bradley and Terry (1952) , avoiding on-policy rollouts. Diffusion-DPO Wallace et al. (2024) adapts this idea to diffusion models by optimizing preferences in the ϵ \bm{\epsilon} -residual space. For unlearning, DUO Park et al. (2024) treats unsafe/safe generations as dispreferred/preferred pairs and introduces a prior-preserving regularizer to maintain utility, while SafetyDPO (AlignGuard) Liu et al. (2025a) uses prompt-conditioned DPO objectives to jointly suppress targeted concepts and preserve non-targeted quality. However, these methods have not been evaluated on FSD models, which we study in this work . PSO Miao et al. (2025) extends preference optimization to FSD models; although not designed for unlearning, we adapt it as a baseline. Beyond diffusion, preference-based unlearning has also shown strong results in large language models Zhang et al. (2024c) ; Fan et al. (2025) ; D’Oosterlinck et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2025b) ; Li et al. (2024) ; Maini et al. (2024) , highlighting its general effectiveness.

sections.heading: Few-step distilled models.
sections.text: FSD diffusion models compress the long sampling trajectory of a base model into only a few-steps (2-8) to achieve fast text-to-image generation. Prominent strategies pursue this goal via different mechanisms: LCMs enforce cross-time agreement ( consistency ) in latent space to enable 2–8 step sampling with strong fidelity Liu et al. (2024) ; Song et al. (2023) ; Turbo variants ( \eg ., SD-Turbo) couple score-distillation sampling Poole et al. (2023) with adversarial losses to sharpen outputs Sauer et al. (2024b) ; Sauer et al. (2024a) . Distribution-matching distillation aligns the student’s output distribution to the teacher using divergence-based objectives Yin et al. (2024b) ; Yin et al. (2024a) . Moreover, recent work on score-matching-based distillation Zhou et al. (2025) ; Chadebec et al. (2025) ; Zhou et al. (2024) and mean-flows Geng et al. (2025) have shown to even surpass the teacher model in terms of image generation quality in few-steps.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we studied post-distillation unlearning for few-step distilled (FSD) text-to-image models, we identified a core mismatch between noise-prediction error-based preference objectives and the few-step generation dynamics of FSD models. We introduced CePU , a consistency-enforced, preference-driven objective that replaces noise-prediction rewards with consistency error rewards aligned with the FSD parameterization.We identified that CePU achieves strong targeted forgetting while preserving overall generation utility, yielding Pareto -optimal trade-offs across identity removal, and nudity unlearning under diverse red-teaming prompts. Moreover, we also provide an extension of our framework to object-level unlearning. Beyond empirical gains, our derivation links preference optimization to per-timestep consistency, providing a stable, tractable surrogate suitable for effective unlearning on few-step distilled models.

sections.text: Diffusion models (DM) learn a data distribution p ⁡ ( 𝒙 0 ) p({\bm{x}}_{0}) by reversing a fixed Markovian noising process of length T T . sections.heading: Consistency Models.
sections.text: The Consistency Model (CM) [ 78 , 54 ] is a generative framework designed for one-step or few-step sampling. Its central idea is to learn a consistency function that maps any point on the probability flow ODE (PF-ODE) trajectory to its origin, \ie , 𝒇 ( t ) : 𝒙 t ↦ 𝒙 0 . {\bm{f}}^{(t)}:{\bm{x}}_{t}\mapsto{\bm{x}}_{0}. A defining property of this function is self-consistency; that is, any two points 𝒙 t {\bm{x}}_{t} and x s x_{s} on the same PF-ODE trajectory [ 79 , 78 ] must map to the same origin: 𝒙 0 = 𝒇 ( t ) ​ ( 𝒙 t ) = 𝒇 ( s ) ​ ( 𝒙 s ) , ∀ t , s ∈ ( 0 , T ] . {\bm{x}}_{0}={\bm{f}}^{(t)}({\bm{x}}_{t})={\bm{f}}^{(s)}({\bm{x}}_{s}),\forall t,s\in(0,T]. (17) The output of a CM/LCM 𝒇 θ ( t ) {\bm{f}}_{\theta}^{(t)} , θ \theta denoting the consistency model weights, is typically parameterized using skip connections [ 2 , 44 ] as: 𝒇 θ ( t ) ​ ( 𝒙 t ) = c skip ​ ( t ) ​ 𝒙 t + c out ​ ( t ) ​ 𝑭 θ ( t ) ​ ( 𝒙 t ) , {\bm{f}}_{\theta}^{(t)}({\bm{x}}_{t})=c_{\text{skip}}(t){\bm{x}}_{t}+c_{\text{out}}(t)\bm{F}_{\theta}^{(t)}({\bm{x}}_{t}), (18) where c skip ​ ( 0 ) = 1 c_{\text{skip}}(0)=1 and c out ​ ( 0 ) = 0 c_{\text{out}}(0)=0 ensure that 𝒇 θ ( 0 ) ​ ( 𝒙 0 ) = 𝒙 0 {\bm{f}}^{(0)}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{0})={\bm{x}}_{0} . Here, 𝑭 θ \bm{F}_{\theta} denotes the approximation of 𝒙 0 {\bm{x}}_{0} at time step t t , defined as: 𝑭 θ ( t ) ​ ( 𝒙 t ) = 𝒙 t − 1 − α t ⋅ ϵ θ ( t ) ​ ( 𝒙 t ) α t ( ϵ ​ -prediction ) , \bm{F}^{(t)}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t})=\frac{{\bm{x}}_{t}-\sqrt{1-\alpha_{t}}\cdot\epsilon_{\theta}^{(t)}({\bm{x}}_{t})}{\sqrt{\alpha_{t}}}\quad(\epsilon\text{-prediction}), (19) CM/LCMs can be obtained either by distilling a standard diffusion model into a few-step equivalent via consistency distillation , or by training a model from scratch using consistency learning . In the distillation setting, an ODE solver Ψ \Psi (typically a DDIM sampler [ 77 ] ) provides a one-step denoised estimate 𝒙 ^ t − k Ψ \hat{{\bm{x}}}_{t-k}^{\Psi} of the noisy sample 𝒙 t ∼ q ⁡ ( 𝒙 t | 𝒙 0 ) {\bm{x}}_{t}\sim q({\bm{x}}_{t}|{\bm{x}}_{0}) , using the teacher’s predicted score. Consistency distillation is then enforced by aligning outputs across steps: ℒ CD ​ ( θ ) = 𝔼 𝒙 t , t ​ [ d ⁡ ( 𝒇 θ ( t ) ​ ( 𝒙 t ) , 𝒇 θ − ( t − k ) ​ ( 𝒙 ^ t − k Ψ ) ) ] , ∀ k ≤ t < T \mathcal{L}_{\text{CD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}_{t},t}\big[d\big({\bm{f}}^{(t)}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}),{\bm{f}}^{(t-k)}_{\theta^{-}}(\hat{{\bm{x}}}_{t-k}^{\Psi})\big)\big],\forall k\leq t<T (20) where θ − \theta^{-} denotes the EMA (or frozen) parameters of θ \theta , and d ⁡ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) d(\cdot,\cdot) is typically the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} squared or Huber distance [ 54 , 78 , 16 ] . The stride k ≥ 1 k\geq 1 specifies the time-step gap used for alignment. sections.heading: Appendix B Probabilistic Sampling Framework for Diffusion Models
sections.text: In diffusion-style generative modeling, the generative process is constructed as an approximation to the reverse of an inference (forward) process. Classical formulations assume a Markovian forward process, but this restriction is unnecessary: what matters is that the forward marginals q ⁡ ( 𝒙 t | 𝒙 0 ) q({\bm{x}}_{t}|{\bm{x}}_{0}) [ 77 ] are preserved, since the diffusion’s learning objectives ( 16 ), ( 20 ), and ( 21 ) do not depend on the joint q ( 𝒙 1 : T | 𝒙 0 ) q({\bm{x}}_{1:T}|{\bm{x}}_{0}) [ 77 ] . Thus, one can construct non-Markovian inference distributions that share the same marginals while admitting richer sampling. We first demonstrate that Diffusion samplers ( \eg , DDPM [ 38 ] , DDIM , [ 77 ] ) and few-step samplers ( \eg , LCM [ 54 ] ) are instances of a single reverse process induced by a non-Markovian forward family that preserves the same marginals [ 77 ] . Demonstrated in Lemma 3 Building on Lemma 3 , which defines the non-Markovian inference distribution q σ ​ ( 𝒙 t − 1 ∣ 𝒙 t , 𝒙 0 ) q_{\sigma}({\bm{x}}_{t-1}\mid{\bm{x}}_{t},{\bm{x}}_{0}) , a trainable generative process p θ ( 𝒙 0 : T ) = p θ ( 𝒙 T ) ∏ t = T 1 p ( t ) ( 𝒙 t − 1 | 𝒙 t ) p_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{0:T})=p_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{T})\prod_{t=T}^{1}p^{(t)}({\bm{x}}_{t-1}|{\bm{x}}_{t}) is defined to replace the intractable true 𝒙 0 {\bm{x}}_{0} . Intuitively, given a noisy input 𝒙 t {\bm{x}}_{t} , the network predicts the underlying clean signal 𝒇 θ ( t ) ​ ( 𝒙 t ) {\bm{f}}_{\theta}^{(t)}({\bm{x}}_{t}) (approximation of OPEN 𝒙 0 ) {\bm{x}}_{0}) , which is then injected into the reverse conditional in Lemma 3 ( 37 ) to yield a sample 𝒙 t − 1 {\bm{x}}_{t-1} . The overall process is defined with prior p θ ​ ( 𝒙 T ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝑰 ) p_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{T})={\mathcal{N}}({\bm{0}},{\bm{I}}) and transitions p θ ( t ) ​ ( 𝒙 t − 1 ∣ 𝒙 t ) = { 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝒇 θ ( 1 ) ​ ( 𝒙 1 ) , σ 1 2 ​ 𝑰 ) , t = 1 , q σ ​ ( 𝒙 t − 1 ∣ 𝒙 t , 𝒇 θ ( t ) ​ ( 𝒙 t ) ) , t > 1 , p_{\theta}^{(t)}({\bm{x}}_{t-1}\mid{\bm{x}}_{t})=\begin{cases}{\mathcal{N}}\big({\bm{f}}_{\theta}^{(1)}({\bm{x}}_{1}),\,\sigma_{1}^{2}{\bm{I}}\big),&t=1,\\ q_{\sigma}\big({\bm{x}}_{t-1}\mid{\bm{x}}_{t},\,{\bm{f}}_{\theta}^{(t)}({\bm{x}}_{t})\big),&t>1,\end{cases} (22) so that the generative process mirrors the structure of the non-Markovian inference family while remaining fully tractable. Gaussian noise at the final step ( t = 1 t{=}1 ) is added to provide support at all time steps. Hence, one obtains 𝒙 t − 1 {\bm{x}}_{t-1} from 𝒙 t {\bm{x}}_{t} via 𝒙 t − 1 = 𝝁 σ ( t ) ​ ( 𝒙 t , 𝒇 θ ( t ) ​ ( 𝒙 t ) ) + σ t ​ ϵ t , ϵ t ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝑰 ) . {\bm{x}}_{t-1}\;=\;\bm{\mu}_{\sigma}^{(t)}\Big({\bm{x}}_{t},{\bm{f}}_{\theta}^{(t)}({\bm{x}}_{t})\Big)\;+\;\sigma_{t}\,\bm{\epsilon}_{t},\quad\bm{\epsilon}_{t}\sim{\mathcal{N}}({\bm{0}},{\bm{I}}). (23) All notations here follow Lemma 1 (Appendix B) of Song \etal [ 77 ] .

sections.heading: Accelerated sampling.
sections.text: The reverse process in ( 23 ) need not be evaluated at every diffusion time step. Since the learning objective depends only on the marginal distributions q ⁡ ( 𝒙 t ∣ 𝒙 0 ) q({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid{\bm{x}}_{0}) , rather than on a particular factorization of the forward process, we may define the inference process over a subsequence of time indices 𝝉 = { τ 1 , τ 2 , … , τ S } , 1 ≤ τ 1 < τ 2 < ⋯ < τ S ≤ T , S ≪ T , \bm{\tau}=\{\tau_{1},\tau_{2},\ldots,\tau_{S}\},\qquad 1\leq\tau_{1}<\tau_{2}<\cdots<\tau_{S}\leq T,\qquad S\ll T, (24) while preserving the same marginals q ⁡ ( 𝒙 τ i ∣ 𝒙 0 ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( α τ i ​ 𝒙 0 , ( 1 − α τ i ) ​ 𝑰 ) . q({\bm{x}}_{\tau_{i}}\mid{\bm{x}}_{0})={\mathcal{N}}\!\left(\sqrt{\alpha_{\tau_{i}}}{\bm{x}}_{0},\,(1-\alpha_{\tau_{i}}){\bm{I}}\right). (25) The corresponding generative process follows the reversed sampling trajectory τ S → τ S − 1 → ⋯ → τ 1 → 0 \tau_{S}\rightarrow\tau_{S-1}\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow\tau_{1}\rightarrow 0 , rather than traversing all T T diffusion steps. For two consecutive elements τ i − 1 < τ i \tau_{i-1}<\tau_{i} of the sampling trajectory, the generalized reverse update can be written as 𝒙 τ i − 1 = \displaystyle{\bm{x}}_{\tau_{i-1}}={} α τ i − 1 ​ 𝒇 θ ( τ i ) ​ ( 𝒙 τ i ) \displaystyle\sqrt{\alpha_{\tau_{i-1}}}\,{\bm{f}}_{\theta}^{(\tau_{i})}({\bm{x}}_{\tau_{i}}) (26) + 1 − α τ i − 1 − σ τ i 2 ​ ( 𝒙 τ i − α τ i ​ 𝒇 θ ( τ i ) ​ ( 𝒙 τ i ) 1 − α τ i ) + σ τ i ​ ϵ i , ϵ i ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝑰 ) . \displaystyle+\sqrt{1-\alpha_{\tau_{i-1}}-\sigma_{\tau_{i}}^{2}}\,\left(\frac{{\bm{x}}_{\tau_{i}}-\sqrt{\alpha_{\tau_{i}}}\,{\bm{f}}_{\theta}^{(\tau_{i})}({\bm{x}}_{\tau_{i}})}{\sqrt{1-\alpha_{\tau_{i}}}}\right)+\sigma_{\tau_{i}}\bm{\epsilon}_{i},\qquad\bm{\epsilon}_{i}\sim{\mathcal{N}}({\bm{0}},{\bm{I}}). (27)

sections.heading: Clean-sample conditional (modeling assumption).
sections.text: The reverse transitions in ( 22 ) and ( 27 ) specify how samples are generated; they do not by themselves define a clean-sample conditional p θ ​ ( 𝒙 0 ∣ 𝒙 t ) p_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{0}\mid{\bm{x}}_{t}) for an arbitrary t t . Following the accelerated variational formulation of DDIM ( [ 77 ] , Appendix C.1), for a sampling subsequence 𝝉 \bm{\tau} with τ S = T \tau_{S}=T and 𝝉 ¯ = { 1 , … , T } ∖ 𝝉 \bar{\bm{\tau}}=\{1,\dots,T\}\setminus\bm{\tau} , the generative model is augmented as p θ ( 𝒙 0 : T ) ≔ p θ ( 𝒙 T ) ∏ i = 1 S p θ ( τ i ) ​ ( 𝒙 τ i − 1 ∣ 𝒙 τ i ) ⏟ transitions used for sampling × ∏ t ∈ 𝝉 ¯ p θ ( t ) ​ ( 𝒙 0 ∣ 𝒙 t ) ⏟ conditionals used in the variational objective , p_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{0:T})\coloneqq p_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{T})\underbrace{\prod_{i=1}^{S}p_{\theta}^{(\tau_{i})}({\bm{x}}_{\tau_{i-1}}\mid{\bm{x}}_{\tau_{i}})}_{\text{transitions used for sampling}}\times\underbrace{\prod_{t\in\bar{\bm{\tau}}}p_{\theta}^{(t)}({\bm{x}}_{0}\mid{\bm{x}}_{t})}_{\text{conditionals used in the variational objective}}, (28) where p θ ( τ i ) ​ ( 𝒙 τ i − 1 ∣ 𝒙 τ i ) = q σ ​ ( 𝒙 τ i − 1 ∣ 𝒙 τ i , 𝒇 θ ( τ i ) ​ ( 𝒙 τ i ) ) p_{\theta}^{(\tau_{i})}({\bm{x}}_{\tau_{i-1}}\mid{\bm{x}}_{\tau_{i}})=q_{\sigma}\big({\bm{x}}_{\tau_{i-1}}\mid{\bm{x}}_{\tau_{i}},{\bm{f}}_{\theta}^{(\tau_{i})}({\bm{x}}_{\tau_{i}})\big) for i ∈ [ S ] i\in[S] , i > 1 i>1 , and p θ ( t ) ​ ( 𝒙 0 ∣ 𝒙 t ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝒙 0 , 𝒇 θ ( t ) ​ ( 𝒙 t ) , σ t 2 ​ 𝑰 ) p_{\theta}^{(t)}({\bm{x}}_{0}\mid{\bm{x}}_{t})={\mathcal{N}}\big({\bm{x}}_{0};{\bm{f}}_{\theta}^{(t)}({\bm{x}}_{t}),\sigma_{t}^{2}{\bm{I}}\big) otherwise ( [ 77 ] , Eqs. 56–57). The clean-sample conditional is thus a separately specified component of the variational model, rather than a conditional obtained by marginalizing or rearranging the reverse sampler. We adopt the same construction: Assumption 1 (Gaussian clean-sample conditional) . For every timestep t t and model ψ ∈ { θ , ϕ } \psi\in\{\theta,\phi\} , p ψ ( t ) ​ ( 𝐱 0 ∣ 𝐱 t ) ≔ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝐱 0 , 𝐟 ψ ( t ) ​ ( 𝐱 t ) , σ t 2 ​ 𝐈 ) p_{\psi}^{(t)}({\bm{x}}_{0}\mid{\bm{x}}_{t})\coloneqq{\mathcal{N}}\big({\bm{x}}_{0};{\bm{f}}_{\psi}^{(t)}({\bm{x}}_{t}),\sigma_{t}^{2}{\bm{I}}\big) , where 𝐟 ψ ( t ) ​ ( 𝐱 t ) {\bm{f}}_{\psi}^{(t)}({\bm{x}}_{t}) is the model’s clean-sample prediction and σ t 2 > 0 \sigma_{t}^{2}>0 is fixed and shared by θ \theta and ϕ \phi . This is the same modeling choice that Diffusion-DPO uses to derive its objective ( [ 85 ] , Supp. S.4). An isotropic Gaussian with fixed variance is a coarse approximation of the true clean-sample posterior, which is in general non-Gaussian and multimodal. We adopt it only to obtain a tractable likelihood-ratio reward, and all results that depend on it (Lemma 4 and Proposition 2 ) are stated conditionally on Assumption 1 .

Diffusion-DPO [ 85 ] arrives at an analogous timestep weighting and sets it to a constant in practice. Doing the same here and absorbing the constant into β \beta when substituting ( 39 ) into ( 1 ) yields the Diffusion-DPO objective ( 2 ). This step replaces the timestep-dependent effective temperature β ​ w t \beta w_{t} by a constant; it changes the per-timestep scale of the preference logit, but not its sign. sections.text: Let c t ≔ 1 / ( 2 ​ σ t 2 ) > 0 c_{t}\coloneqq 1/(2\sigma_{t}^{2})>0 , and define L ≔ ∑ j = 1 m Δ θ C ​ ( 𝒙 t j ) , X ≔ ∑ j < k ( ⟨ δ θ , j , δ θ , k ⟩ − ⟨ δ ϕ , j , δ ϕ , k ⟩ ) L\coloneqq\sum_{j=1}^{m}\Delta_{\theta}^{\textup{C}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j}}),\qquad X\coloneqq\sum_{j<k}\Big(\langle\delta_{\theta,j},\delta_{\theta,k}\rangle-\langle\delta_{\phi,j},\delta_{\phi,k}\rangle\Big) (73) as the timestep-local and cross-timestep contributions, respectively. The cross-timestep term couples consistency increments evaluated at different timesteps. Consequently, unlike the timestep-local term, it is not directly available from a single sampled adjacent transition. Retaining only the local contribution therefore yields a reward that can be evaluated using the same stochastic, per-timestep sampling procedure employed during DPO training. Three consequences follow: • Exactness for a one-step decomposition. If the entire interval from t 0 = 0 t_{0}=0 to t m = t t_{m}=t consists of a single increment ( m = 1 m=1 ), the sum over j < k j<k is empty. Hence X = 0 X=0 and l ~ θ = l θ \tilde{l}_{\theta}=l_{\theta} . • Sign agreement under bounded cross-timestep interactions. A sufficient condition for l ~ θ \tilde{l}_{\theta} and l θ l_{\theta} to have the same sign is 2 ​ | X | < | L | 2|X|<|L| . Because the preferred and dispreferred samples share the same timestep t t , and hence the same c t c_{t} (Algorithm 1 ), l θ ​ ( 𝒙 0 + | 𝒙 t + ) − l θ ​ ( 𝒙 0 − | 𝒙 t − ) = − c t ​ [ ( L + − L − ) + 2 ​ ( X + − X − ) ] , l_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{0}^{+}|{\bm{x}}_{t}^{+})-l_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{0}^{-}|{\bm{x}}_{t}^{-})=-c_{t}\Big[(L^{+}-L^{-})+2(X^{+}-X^{-})\Big], whereas the corresponding surrogate margin is − c t ​ ( L + − L − ) . -c_{t}(L^{+}-L^{-}). Thus, a sufficient condition for the two margins to have the same sign is 2 ​ | X + − X − | < | L + − L − | . 2|X^{+}-X^{-}|<|L^{+}-L^{-}|. • No unconditional guarantee. Without additional assumptions on X X , the signs of the exact and surrogate rewards need not agree. For example, take m = 2 m=2 , scalar increments, σ t 2 = 1 \sigma_{t}^{2}=1 , δ θ = ( 1 , − 1 ) \delta_{\theta}=(1,-1) , and δ ϕ = ( 0 , 1 ) \delta_{\phi}=(0,1) . Then L = ( 1 2 + ( − 1 ) 2 ) − ( 0 2 + 1 2 ) = 1 , X = ( 1 ) ​ ( − 1 ) − ( 0 ) ​ ( 1 ) = − 1 . L=(1^{2}+(-1)^{2})-(0^{2}+1^{2})=1,\qquad X=(1)(-1)-(0)(1)=-1. Hence, the exact reward is l θ = − 1 2 ​ ( L + 2 ​ X ) = + 1 2 , l_{\theta}=-\tfrac{1}{2}(L+2X)=+\tfrac{1}{2}, whereas the surrogate is l ~ θ = − 1 2 ​ L = − 1 2 . \tilde{l}_{\theta}=-\tfrac{1}{2}L=-\tfrac{1}{2}. Here 2 ​ | X | = 2 > | L | = 1 2|X|=2>|L|=1 , so the sufficient sign-agreement condition is violated. We therefore interpret l ~ θ \tilde{l}_{\theta} as a timestep-local surrogate obtained by retaining the local component of the exact likelihood-ratio decomposition while discarding cross-timestep interactions. In general, this truncation does not guarantee equality with, or even sign agreement with, the exact likelihood ratio; the sufficient conditions above characterize cases in which sign agreement is preserved. Accordingly, CePU does not rely on Proposition 2 for a convergence or optimality guarantee. Rather, the proposition provides a likelihood-based motivation for the local consistency reward used by CePU , whose effectiveness is evaluated empirically in Section 3 and Appendix F .

sections.heading: Appendix D Directly Unlearning on FSD Model
sections.text: Table A : Direct unlearning on the few-step distilled (FSD) model (SD1.5-Distilled → \rightarrow Unlearning ) vs. a two-stage pipeline that first unlearns the base diffusion model and then distills it (SD1.5 → \rightarrow Unlearning → \rightarrow Distillation). Metrics SD1.5 SD1.5 → \rightarrow Unlearning SD1.5 → \rightarrow Unlearning → \rightarrow Distillation ( 15 mins + 24 hours ) SD1.5-Distilled SD1.5-Distilled → \rightarrow Unlearning ( 15 mins ) Buttocks 18 0 1 15 0 Female Breast 252 19 17 253 17 Female Genitalia 10 1 1 12 1 Male Genitalia 11 1 1 10 1 Anus 0 0 0 0 0 I2P NudeNet Detections ( ↓ \downarrow ) Total 291 21 20 290 19 CLIP Score ( ↑ \uparrow ) 0.31660 0.31271 0.30258 0.30235 0.30232 A natural approach to bring in safety interventions to few-step FSD models is to first perform unlearning on the base diffusion model (BM) and then distill the edited BM into an FSD model. However, this two-stage pipeline incurs substantial computational overhead due to the expensive distillation process. In contrast, we directly apply CePU to the FSD model. As shown in Table A , direct unlearning on FSD model using CePU achieves performance comparable to the two-stage pipeline in terms of both unlearning effectiveness and utility preservation. Crucially, it avoids the costly distillation step. In our case we distill a SD1.5 model, using LCM distillation, for ∼ 24 \sim 24 hours on 4×A5000 GPUs (24GB each), noting that distillation can be run longer to further improve generation quality. In contrast, CePU performs unlearning in ∼ 15 \sim 15 minutes on a single A5000 GPU. This results in orders-of-magnitude lower time and computational overhead compared to unlearning followed by distillation while directly editing the deployed FSD model, making the approach both efficient and aligned with deployment-time objectives. The unlearning on the SD1.5 prior to unlearning is conducted using DUO [ 61 ] .

sections.heading: Appendix E Training and Evaluation Details
sections.text: For all preference-driven unlearning baselines, including DPO [ 85 ] , DUO [ 61 ] , PSO [ 58 ] , SafetyDPO [ 50 ] , and CePU , we fine-tune using LoRA [ 39 ] with rank 32 and the AdamW optimizer. Following prior work, we do not apply LoRA to the cross-attention layers to avoid overfitting to specific text prompts [ 61 , 24 ] . As in [ 61 ] , since β \beta linearly scales the learning rate at initialization, we rescale the learning rate by dividing it by the same factor whenever β \beta is increased. Using β = 100 \beta=100 as our default setting, we adopt a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} and a batch size of 4. We found that a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} with β = 100 \beta=100 reliably removes the target concept across all preference-driven unlearning frameworks; therefore, we use this configuration as our base setup and then modulate β \beta and the learning rate \wrt β \beta , as discussed, consistently for all methods. Moreover, our proposed CePU objective uses the consistency error as a proxy reward. To compute the consistency error, we sample a time t j t_{j} and set t j − 1 t_{j-1} to a fixed offset k k such that t j − 1 = t j − k t_{j-1}=t_{j}-k , for ease of implementation and efficiency. For our experiments, we set k = 20 k=20 following [ 54 ] . Using this setup, we train all methods for 500 iterations for both the nudity and identity unlearning tasks. The preference-driven baselines require no more than 15 minutes to fine-tune the FSD models for 500 iterations on a workstation with an AMD EPYC 7413 24-core CPU, 512 GB RAM, and 4 NVIDIA A5000 GPUs. For evaluating all unlearning methods by generating images from the models after conducting the unlearning. Primarily we sample image for 4 steps with LCM scheduler [ 54 ] with classifier-free guidance scale of 0 (disabled).

sections.heading: E.1 Training Dataset Creation
sections.text: Following [ 61 ] , we construct paired samples ( 𝒙 0 + , 𝒙 0 − ) ({\bm{x}}_{0}^{+},{\bm{x}}_{0}^{-}) with SDEdit [ 57 ] to obtain 𝒙 0 + {\bm{x}}_{0}^{+} from 𝒙 0 − {\bm{x}}_{0}^{-} by removing undesirable concepts while preserving non-target semantics. For each unsafe concept 𝒄 − {\bm{c}}^{-} , we first generate an undesirable image 𝒙 0 − {\bm{x}}_{0}^{-} ; then produce a desirable counterpart 𝒙 0 + {\bm{x}}_{0}^{+} by applying SDEdit to 𝒙 0 − {\bm{x}}_{0}^{-} at a mid-range noise level τ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \tau\in(0,1) using the preferred prompt 𝒄 + {\bm{c}}^{+} . Specifically, we use τ = 0.6 \tau=0.6 , \ie , 60% strength, given there are original 1000 diffusion steps. This procedure preserves global scene semantics while modifying only concept-specific attributes. We use these pairs as selective counterfactual supervision for preference optimization across all preference-driven unlearning baselines [ 85 , 61 , 50 , 58 ] , including CePU for our analysis. In Table B and C we provide the training examples that we generate using ChatGPT [ 1 ] used to generate these pairs for the celebrity unlearning task, inspired by [ 46 ] . For nudity unlearning we use the prompts directly sampled by [ 46 ] as shown in Table D . For object-level unlearning we do not use the SDEdit procedure, rather we sample images using the prompt a picture of <class-name> .

sections.heading: E.3 Identity Unlearning
sections.text: For identity unlearning, we generate 64 64 images using the 64 64 prompts listed in Tables B and C for a target identity. Using SDEdit, we construct counterfactual training pairs by editing each generated image with a corresponding identity-agnostic prompt, where the identity keyword is replaced with a neutral term ( \eg , a man or a woman ). This training data creation protocol is followed by all preference-based methods [ 85 , 61 , 58 , 50 ] including CePU , rather the same sampled dataset is used to ensure a fair, head-to-head comparison of the unlearning performance. Examples shown in Figure A . For evaluation, we use a disjoint set of 64 64 test prompt templates containing the target identity to generate images and measure target-identity accuracy ( 𝒜 target \mathcal{A}_{\text{target}} ) using the GCD (Giphy-Celeb-Detector) classifier [ 31 ] . To assess utility preservation, we also generate 64 64 images using the identity-agnostic versions of the test prompts and compute LPIPS \mathrm{LPIPS} with respect to the FSD baseline. Finally, to evaluate unintended degradation on other identities, we generate 64 64 images for each of four non-target celebrities (Gal Gadot, Scarlett Johansson, Bradley Cooper, and Jake Gyllenhaal) and report the average recognition accuracy ( 𝒜 other \mathcal{A}_{\text{other}} ) using the GCD classifier. Note that during unlearning we do not explicitly enforce retention of other identities; the retention loss is computed only using identity-agnostic prompts and images. Nonetheless, all methods considered in our study, including preference-based [ 85 , 61 , 58 , 50 ] , zero-shot [ 95 , 25 ] , and fine-tuning approaches [ 24 , 47 , 83 ] , are evaluated using the same protocol described above. sections.heading: E.4 Nudity Unlearning
sections.text: For nudity unlearning, following Ko \etal [ 46 ] , we construct 800 800 paired prompts ( 𝒄 + , 𝒄 − ) ({\bm{c}}^{+},{\bm{c}}^{-}) where 𝒄 − {\bm{c}}^{-} contains nudity-enforcing keywords and 𝒄 + {\bm{c}}^{+} is obtained by removing the nudity-specific terms while preserving the remaining prompt structure. Unsafe training samples are first generated using the 800 800 nudity-enforcing prompts introduced by Ko \etal [ 46 ] (examples shown in Table D ), after which a counterfactual preference pair is constructed for each sample using the corresponding sanitized prompt. Paired preference images ( 𝒙 0 + , 𝒙 0 − ) ({\bm{x}}_{0}^{+},{\bm{x}}_{0}^{-}) are generated using SDEdit [ 57 ] as described in Section 2.5 , enabling controlled semantic edits while preserving the underlying scene composition and visual structure. Representative examples are shown in Figure B . This paired-data construction protocol is consistently adopted across all preference-based baselines [ 85 , 61 , 58 , 50 ] , including CePU , and the same sampled dataset is used across all preference-based methods to ensure a fair, head-to-head comparison. For evaluation, we assess unlearning effectiveness using NudeNet detections [ 59 ] by counting exposed-body-part predictions, including Female Genitalia, Male Genitalia, Female Breast, Buttocks, and Anus, on red-teaming benchmarks from prior work: Inappropriate Image Prompts (I2P) [ 73 ] , Ring-A-Bell (RAB) [ 84 ] , SneakyPrompts (SP) [ 92 ] , Prompt4Debugging (P4D) [ 13 ] , and Multi-Modal Attack (MMA) [ 91 ] , including both adversarial (MMA-A) and sanitized (MMA-S) variants. None of these evaluation prompts are used during training. We report Defense Success Rate (DSR), defined as the percentage reduction in NudeNet detections relative to the original FSD model. To evaluate utility preservation after unlearning, we additionally compute CLIP Score (CS) [ 37 ] and LPIPS \mathrm{LPIPS} [ 100 ] on 1000 1000 benign LAION prompts [ 74 ] sampled following [ 91 ] . Nonetheless, all methods considered in our study, including preference-based [ 85 , 61 , 58 , 50 ] , zero-shot [ 95 , 25 ] , and fine-tuning approaches [ 24 , 47 , 83 ] , are evaluated using the same protocol described above. sections.heading: E.5 Object-level Unlearning
sections.text: For object-level unlearning, we generate 90 90 images per class (using different random seeds) with the prompt template a picture of <class-name> , where <class-name> corresponds to classes from Imagenette or the fine-grained object categories introduced in [ 83 ] . During training, one class is designated as the target concept to be unlearned, while all remaining classes are treated as concepts to be retained. This training data creation protocol is followed by all preference-based methods [ 85 , 61 , 58 , 50 ] including CePU , rather the same sampled dataset is used to ensure a fair, head-to-head comparison of the unlearning performance. For evaluation, we generate 500 500 images per class (with different seeds) using a distinct prompt template Image of <class-name> . We report the target-class accuracy ( 𝒜 target \mathcal{A}_{\text{target}} ), the average accuracy on non-target classes ( 𝒜 other \mathcal{A}_{\text{other}} ), and the harmonic mean ( ℋ mean \mathcal{H}_{\text{mean}} ) between 1 − 𝒜 target 1-\mathcal{A}_{\text{target}} and 𝒜 other \mathcal{A}_{\text{other}} . To assess utility preservation, we also compute LPIPS \mathrm{LPIPS} on samples generated from non-target classes relative to the FSD baseline. This setup is applied to both Imagenette class unlearning (Tables 3 and E and F ) and fine-grained object unlearning (Table G ). Nonetheless, all methods considered in our study, including preference-based [ 85 , 61 , 58 , 50 ] , zero-shot [ 95 , 25 ] , and fine-tuning approaches [ 24 , 47 , 83 ] , are evaluated using the same protocol described above.

sections.heading: F.1 Additional Object-Level Unlearning on Imagenette.
sections.text: We additionally benchmark object-level unlearning on the 10 Imagenette classes against both zero-shot-based and preference-driven baselines in Tables E and F . CePU achieves complete removal for all target classes, driving the average target accuracy 𝒜 target \mathcal{A}_{\text{target}} to 0.00 0.00 , while maintaining strong retention on non-target classes ( 𝒜 other = 60.85 ) (\mathcal{A}_{\text{other}}=60.85) with low perceptual drift from the original FSD model (LPIPS = 0.0900 =0.0900 ). Note that, 𝒜 o ​ t ​ h ​ e ​ r \mathcal{A}_{other} for these experiments are the average across classes not being unlearned. Compared to zero-shot alternatives, UCE [ 25 ] provides reasonably strong unlearning but at substantially higher perceptual distortion (LPIPS = 0.2894 =0.2894 ), while SAFREE [ 95 ] degrades both removal and retention performance. Compared to preference-based methods for which we adopt a similar strategy as discussed in 3.3 to avoid ambiguity of preferred counter-part examples, DUO [ 61 ] preserves image statistics well (LPIPS = 0.0630 =0.0630 ) but fails to fully erase target concepts ( 𝒜 target = 14.52 ) (\mathcal{A}_{\text{target}}=14.52) ; PSO [ 58 ] and SafetyDPO [ 50 ] show larger trade-offs between removal and retention, and DPO [ 85 ] exhibits the weakest overall balance. Overall, CePU obtains the highest harmonic mean ( ℋ mean = 75.66 ) (\mathcal{H}_{\text{mean}}=75.66) across all methods, demonstrating that it delivers the most favorable trade-off between precise object removal and preservation of non-target classes. In Section F , the preference-driven baselines (DPO, DUO, PSO, and SafetyDPO) are reported with β = 100 \beta=100 , corresponding to their best 𝒜 target \mathcal{A}_{\text{target}} reduction. To evaluate this property, we analyze the retention of dog breeds that are semantically adjacent to the targeted concept German Shepherd , that include Malinois , Rottweiler , Norwegian Elkhound , Labrador Retriever , and Golden Retriever as identified by [ 83 ] . G reports the classification accuracy and LPIPS distance relative to the FSD model for target and these adjacent concepts after unlearning. The target concept accuracy 𝒜 target \mathcal{A}_{\text{target}} measures the effectiveness of unlearning (lower is better), while 𝒜 other \mathcal{A}_{\text{other}} and LPIPS quantify the retention of adjacent concepts, where higher 𝒜 other \mathcal{A}_{\text{other}} and lower LPIPS indicate better preservation. Our method achieves complete removal of the target concept ( 𝒜 target = 0 \mathcal{A}_{\text{target}}=0 ) while preserving adjacent concepts more effectively than FADE [ 83 ] , achieving higher average accuracy (77.76 % vs. 75.28 %) and lower perceptual deviation from the base model (LPIPS 0.0568 vs. 0.0790). These results suggest that CePU performs more targeted concept removal, mitigating unintended collateral degradation of semantically related concepts. The CePU numbers are provided for β = 500 \beta=500 and λ = 10 \lambda=10 .

sections.heading: F.3 Extended Identity Unlearning Results.
sections.text: Tables, H and I extend the identity-unlearning comparison by reporting results for preference-based methods across multiple β \beta values on DS-V8-LCM [ 19 ] and DS-V7-LCM [ 18 ] . Consistent with the role of β \beta , we observe a clear unlearning–utility trade-off: lower β \beta enforces stronger forgetting but often degrades preservation of other identities, while higher β \beta improves retention at the expense of weaker target suppression. Across both targets and both FSD backbones, CePU traces a stronger Pareto frontier than prior preference-based approaches, achieving superior balance between 𝒜 target \mathcal{A}_{\text{target}} and 𝒜 others \mathcal{A}_{\text{others}} . In particular, on DS-V8-LCM, CePU attains complete removal for all reported β \beta values while substantially improving non-target retention as β \beta increases, leading to the best harmonic mean at β = 1000 \beta{=}1000 . On DS-V7-LCM, where the task is comparatively harder, CePU remains robust and competitive across β \beta , again offering strong controllability over the trade-off. These results reinforce that CePU is not tied to a narrow hyperparameter regime and consistently yields favorable identity-unlearning performance across settings. sections.heading: F.4 Extended Nudity Unlearning Results.
sections.text: We further report nudity-unlearning results across multiple β \beta values for preference-based methods on DS-V8-LCM [ 19 ] , DS-V7-LCM [ 18 ] , and SD-Turbo [ 75 ] in Tables J , L , and K . Across all three backbones, β \beta induces a clear safety–utility trade-off: low β \beta strongly suppresses unsafe generations, whereas high β \beta better preserves the original model distribution but weakens unlearning. Despite this trade-off, CePU consistently lies on a more favorable frontier than prior preference-based baselines. On DS-V8-LCM and DS-V7-LCM, CePU with β = 100 \beta{=}100 achieves the strongest suppression, reducing total NudeNet detections from 3120 to 61 and from 2554 to 68, corresponding to 98.04% and 97.34% DSR, respectively. On SD-Turbo, CePU is even stronger: β = 250 \beta{=}250 achieves the best overall suppression with only 5 total detections and 99.43% DSR, while β = 500 \beta{=}500 provides a particularly attractive trade-off, retaining near-identical suppression (6 detections, 99.32% DSR) with substantially improved LPIPS and CLIP alignment. By contrast, alternative preference-based methods deteriorate sharply as β \beta increases, often approaching the unsafe baseline while only improving perceptual similarity. These results reinforce that CePU is robust across backbones and hyperparameter settings, and provides effective control over the safety–utility trade-off in nudity unlearning. sections.heading: Appendix G Limitations
sections.text: We view our scope and design choices as opportunities for future extension for unlearning in FSD models. In this work, we focus on two salient safety axes, celebrity identity and NSFW nudity, on a representative subset of few-step distilled models (DreamShaper-V7-LCM, DreamShaper-V8-LCM, SD-Turbo), leaving broader harms ( \eg , violence, hate, or self-harm content), multilingual or code-mixed prompts, and simultaneous multi-concept unlearning as natural directions for follow-up studies. We rely on established automatic proxies, NudeNet [ 59 ] , a celebrity face-ID classifier (Giphy celebrity detector) [ 31 ] , LPIPS [ 100 ] , and CLIPScore [ 37 ] , which provide scalable, quantitative evaluation but are inherently imperfect and potentially biased, highlighting the value of further complementing CePU with human studies or richer safety benchmarks. Likewise, we report results under a fixed set of hyperparameters ( \eg , learning rate, LoRA rank [ 39 , 64 ] , unlearning strength β \beta , retention weight λ \lambda ) tuned to a limited set of tasks, which simplifies comparison across methods and suggests future work on systematic sensitivity analyses or automated hyperparameter selection for different deployment regimes. Moreover, as future steps, we seek to adopt our setup to enable continual unlearning [ 82 , 30 , 29 , 76 , 36 ] .

sections.heading: Appendix H Broader Impacts
sections.text: Text-to-image unlearning has the potential to improve the safe and responsible deployment of generative models by enabling the suppression of harmful, explicit, privacy-sensitive, or copyrighted content without requiring expensive retraining from scratch. Such methods may help mitigate misuse involving non-consensual imagery, public identity impersonation, unsafe content generation, and regulatory non-compliance, while providing a computationally efficient mechanism for post-deployment alignment of large generative models. However, these methods also introduce important societal risks. Selective concept removal may unintentionally suppress legitimate artistic, educational, or cultural expression, and poorly designed unlearning objectives may amplify demographic or representational biases. Furthermore, unlearning mechanisms could themselves be misused for targeted censorship or ideological suppression. Additionally, unlearning does not guarantee complete removal of harmful behavior, particularly under adversarial prompting or paraphrased queries. We therefore believe that text-to-image unlearning should be developed and deployed alongside careful evaluation, transparency, and human oversight.

Corresponding author: pate1332@purdue.edu . Jun Fang Affiliation: Amazon AGI Greg Ver Steeg Affiliation: Amazon AGI Qiang Qiu Sravan Sripada Affiliation: Amazon AGI [1pt] Purdue University Abstract Text-to-image diffusion models are increasingly distilled into few-step variants and being deployed to enable fast inference. However, their ability to generate harmful or undesired content poses significant safety risks. Data-driven unlearning methods suppress targeted generations by fine-tuning model weights using specialized unlearning objectives. Crucially, these objectives implicitly rely on multi-step denoising dynamics, an assumption that breaks down for few-step distilled (FSD) models, resulting in ineffective forgetting. Furthermore, performing unlearning on the non-distilled base model and subsequently re-distilling it to obtain an unlearned FSD model incurs substantial computational and time overhead, making it impractical in many settings. Hence, we address this limitation with a preference-driven unlearning framework that revisits Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) for diffusion models. We show that standard DPO and its unlearning derivatives, formulated around noise-prediction error, transfer poorly to FSD models due to their altered generation dynamics. To overcome this, we introduce a modified preference optimization formulation explicitly aligned with the few-step generation properties, enabling direct concept removal in FSD models while preserving few-step efficiency and maintaining strong retention of desirable (non-targeted) capabilities. We evaluate our framework primarily on identity and NSFW (nudity) removal tasks and also extend our method to object-level unlearning. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent and effective forgetting, and strong retention performance, establishing our method as a practical and principled solution for unlearning in FSD models. 1 Introduction Text-to-image ( T2I ) diffusion models underpin modern generative visual synthesis, enabling high-quality and controllable image generation Zhang et al. (2023) ; Saharia et al. (2022) ; Rombach et al. (2022) ; Pernias et al. (2023) . However, their success has amplified concerns about undesirable generations Park et al. (2024) ; Birhane et al. (2023) ; Rando et al. (2022) ; Schramowski et al. (2023) ; Golatkar et al. (2024) , driven by unsafe or identity-specific content in large-scale training data Schuhmann et al. (2022) . Open-weight Stable Diffusion ( SD ) models Rombach et al. (2022) , widely accessible via HuggingFace [ 42 ] , can generate celebrity identities or not-safe-for-work ( NSFW ) content such as nudity. Safety filters are often bypassable via prompt obfuscation or multilingual cues Yang et al. (2024a) ; Liu et al. (2024) ; Schramowski et al. (2023) ; Tsai et al. (2024) ; Yang et al. (2024b) , motivating targeted unlearning to remove specific concepts while preserving utility Bourtoule et al. (2021) ; Liu et al. (2024) ; Gandikota et al. (2023) ; Gandikota et al. (2024) ; Park et al. (2024) ; Fan et al. (2023) ; Ko et al. (2024) ; Wu and Harandi (2025) ; Patel and Qiu (2025) ; Wu and Harandi (2024) ; Gong et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2024d) . Concurrently, T2I models are distilled into few-step variants Song et al. (2023) ; Luo et al. (2023) ; Sauer et al. (2024b) ; Sauer et al. (2024a) ; Yin et al. (2024b) ; Yin et al. (2024a) ; Chadebec et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2024) ; Zhou et al. (2025) ; Zhou et al. (2024) ; Chen et al. (2025a) for efficient inference. These few-step distilled ( FSD ) models reduce sampling from 50–100 sampling steps Rombach et al. (2022) ; Song et al. (2021) to 2–8 steps, typically via student reparameterization and teacher-guided training Song et al. (2023) ; Luo et al. (2023) . This alters generation dynamics: FSD models commit early with limited intermediate exploration (Figure 1 A ). Also, undesirable concept residues from the base model ( BM ) can transfer to, and even be amplified in, FSD models (Figure 1 B ), making post-distillation safety critical. Figure 1 : A. LPIPS-to-final vs. timesteps for the base model (BM) [ 20 ] and its few-step distilled (FSD) variant [ 19 ] . BM follows long, weakly constrained trajectories, while FSD shows steep LPIPS decay, committing within a few steps, limiting mid-path adaptability. B. Severity of unsafe generations in FSD. FSD model shows elevated detections pre-unlearning compared to its BM, which our method markedly reduces. C. SD-Turbo [ 75 ] unlearning dynamics . Our method (last row) based on consistency error shows stable, gradual and effective unlearning during the course of training. A naïve solution—first unlearning on the BM and then re-distilling—assumes that unlearning effects transfer faithfully through the distillation process Luo et al. (2023) ; Yin et al. (2024a) , an assumption that is not guaranteed in practice Suriyakumar et al. (2025) ; George et al. (2025a) . Moreover, this pipeline incurs substantial computational overhead ( \eg , Luo \etal Luo et al. (2023) report 32 A100 GPU hours, while Yin \etal Yin et al. (2024a) report 36 hours on 72 A100 GPUs). Since the FSD model is ultimately the deployed artifact, it is both necessary and desirable to directly unlearn undesirable properties on the FSD model itself. Preference-based methods such as direct unlearning optimization ( DUO ) Park et al. (2024) and SafetyDPO (AlignGuard) Liu et al. (2025a) that are based on direct-preference optimization ( DPO ) Rafailov et al. (2023) ; Wallace et al. (2024) have shown robust Park et al. (2024) and scalable Liu et al. (2025a) T2I unlearning while enabling fine-grained control Park et al. (2024) ; Helbling et al. (2025) , by contrasting preferred and dispreferred samples using noise-prediction errors along denoising trajectories. However, this formulation assumes full-step diffusion with long trajectories Zhang et al. (2025) and noise-based parameterization Ho et al. (2020) ; Song et al. (2021) ; Rombach et al. (2022) . When applied to FSD models, characterized by few-step generation and different parameterization Luo et al. (2023) ; Karras et al. (2022) , this assumption breaks, yielding ineffective unlearning, see Figure 1 C . We identify this objective dissonance as the key bottleneck. We propose C onsistency- e nforced P reference-driven U nlearning ( CePU ), a framework tailored to FSD models. Instead of noise-prediction error Wallace et al. (2024) , CePU (C-P-U) uses consistency error Song et al. (2023) , \ie , the discrepancy between final timestep predictions from adjacent noisy timesteps, capturing the intrinsic few-step inductive bias Chen et al. (2025b) ; Song et al. (2023) . This consistency error serves as an implicit reward signal, which is minimized for preferred samples and maximized for dispreferred ones, aligning preference learning with FSD dynamics. Notably, directly unlearning on the FSD model achieves performance comparable to unlearning on the BM followed by distillation (Appendix D ), while requiring only ≈ 15 \approx 15 minutes on a single A5000 GPU, highlighting the practicality of post-distillation unlearning. We evaluate CePU on identity removal and nudity suppression, including red-teaming prompts Tsai et al. (2024) ; Yang et al. (2024a) ; Yang et al. (2024b) ; Chin et al. (2024) ; Schramowski et al. (2023) . Since FSD models can generate unsafe content even without explicit prompts (Figure 5 ), this provides a stringent testbed. We further analyze utility–unlearning trade-offs and extend CePU to object-level unlearning. Combining targeted preference-driven suppression with this utility-preserving constraint gives the final CePU objective: ℒ CePU ​ ( θ ) = ℒ C-DPO ​ ( θ ) + λ ​ ℒ RET ​ ( θ ) , \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{CePU}}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_{\texttt{C-DPO}}(\theta)+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\texttt{RET}}(\theta), (14) where λ \lambda controls the utility–unlearning Pareto frontier (Section 3.4 ). While ℒ C-DPO \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{C-DPO}} suppresses undesirable generations through consistency-aware preference optimization, ℒ RET \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{RET}} preserves few-step fidelity on non-target concepts, enabling selective unlearning without unnecessarily degrading model utility. Figure 2 B summarizes the overall CePU framework. In practice, the adjacent states 𝒙 t j {\bm{x}}_{t_{j}} and 𝒙 t j − 1 {\bm{x}}_{t_{j-1}} , with t j − 1 = t j − k t_{j-1}=t_{j}-k , are obtained by forward-noising the same clean sample 𝒙 0 {\bm{x}}_{0} using a shared noise realization ϵ \epsilon . This isolates the change across timesteps from variation due to independently sampled noise. The lower-noise prediction 𝒇 θ ( t j − 1 ) ​ ( 𝒙 t j − 1 , 𝒄 ) {\bm{f}}_{\theta}^{(t_{j-1})}({\bm{x}}_{t_{j-1}},{\bm{c}}) is treated as a stop-gradient target, so optimization updates the prediction at t j t_{j} toward a stable adjacent-step target rather than allowing both sides of the consistency relation to move simultaneously.
